about: Asking Social Security to accept an appeal after the 60-day limit (good cause).

rows.plain: You generally have 60 days from the date you received a decision letter to ask for an appeal.
Social Security assumes you received the letter 5 days after the date on it, unless you show it arrived later.
If the last day falls on a weekend or national holiday, the deadline moves to the next workday.
If the time limit has passed, you can still ask for the appeal. The request for more time must be in writing and say why it is late.

Social Security looks at what kept you from filing on time, whether its own action misled you, whether a change in the law confused you, and any physical, mental, educational or language limitation, including limited English.
The same good-cause rule applies to SSI decisions.
A serious illness kept you from contacting Social Security in any way, even through someone else.
There was a death or serious illness in your immediate family.
Important records were destroyed or damaged by fire or another accident.
You were trying hard to find information you needed, but could not find it in time.
You asked Social Security to explain the decision before the deadline, and you appeal within 60 days of getting the explanation (30 days if you are asking the Appeals Council or going to court).
Social Security gave you wrong or incomplete information about how or when to appeal.
You never received the decision letter.
You sent the request on time to another government agency in good faith, and it reached Social Security late.
A physical, mental, educational or language limitation kept you from filing on time or from knowing about the deadline.
Something unusual or unavoidable kept you from filing on time or from knowing you needed to.
